Ethics vs. morals: a useful distinction

In everyday use, "ethics" and "morals" are used as synonyms. In philosophy, it's useful to distinguish them: morals are the concrete rules and values a person or culture holds ("don't lie," "help those in need"). Ethics is the philosophical study of those rules: why are they correct? how do we justify them? what do we do when they conflict?

This course is about ethics in that second sense: it's not going to give you a list of rules, it's going to give you tools to examine any rule you already have.

Why this isn't "just opinion"

It's common to hear "morality is subjective, everyone has their own." There's some truth there — different cultures and people do value different things. But that doesn't mean all moral arguments are equally good. Just as in math there are better and worse ways to reason even when people make different mistakes, in ethics there are more and less consistent arguments, even though disagreement exists.

The course map

  • The three major schools (classes 2-4): judging by consequences, by duties, or by character.
  • The relativism debate (class 5): is there a universal morality, or does it all depend on culture?
  • Real dilemmas (classes 6-7): applying the schools to hard cases, including the ethics of technology.
  • Wrap-up (class 8): build your own moral compass, with tools, not borrowed certainties.
💡 Throughout the course you'll notice the Ancient Wizard won't tell you "this is right" or "this is wrong" — he'll ask you why you think what you think. That's the method, not a dodge.

0d7eda45c4084e:
Duty above outcome

Deontology (from the Greek deon, "duty") holds that certain actions are right or wrong in themselves, regardless of their consequences. Its most influential formulation comes from Immanuel Kant (1724-1804).

The categorical imperative

Kant proposed a test for knowing whether an action is morally right: ask yourself whether you could want everyone to act according to the same rule you're about to follow. If the rule becomes incoherent or self-defeating when universalized, it's wrong.

🧪 Example: "I'm going to lie to get what I want." If EVERYONE lied whenever it suited them, the trust that makes communication possible would collapse — no one would believe anyone. The rule defeats itself when universalized, so Kant concludes lying is wrong, regardless of the outcome in a particular case.

People as ends, not means

Another key formulation from Kant: always treat people as ends in themselves, never merely as means to your own purposes. This is what makes using someone — lying to them, manipulating them, exploiting them — wrong even if the final outcome "benefits more people."

The most common criticism

⚠️ The problem: absolute rules sometimes clash with each other, or produce outcomes almost no one would accept. Kant himself held that lying is wrong even to protect someone from a murderer asking where they're hiding — a conclusion most people, including many philosophers, reject.
💡 Consequentialism asks "what outcome does this produce?" Deontology asks "what kind of rule am I following?" The next school asks something different: "what kind of person does this make me?"

1f54e6506731c7:
A different question

While consequentialism asks "what outcome does this produce?" and deontology asks "what rule am I following?", virtue ethics — originating with Aristotle (384-322 BC) — asks something different: "what kind of person do I want to be?" The idea is that by repeatedly acting well, you develop virtues (courage, honesty, generosity), and a truly virtuous person acts well naturally, without needing to calculate consequences or consult rules for every decision.

The golden mean

Aristotle proposed that every virtue is a midpoint between two vices — one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage, for example, is the midpoint between cowardice (deficiency) and recklessness (excess of courage without prudence).

⚖️ More examples of the golden mean:
  • Generosity = midpoint between stinginess and extravagance.
  • Self-confidence = midpoint between insecurity and arrogance.
  • Honesty = midpoint between being brutally cruel with the truth and lying for comfort.

Virtue as habit, not rule

For Aristotle, virtue isn't learned by reading rules — it's cultivated by practicing it, just like learning a craft. You become courageous by repeatedly acting with courage, not by memorizing a definition of courage.

💡 The three schools aren't necessarily mutually exclusive: many people use all three, depending on the situation. Good moral reasoning sometimes combines "what outcome does this produce?", "what rule am I following?" and "what kind of person does this make me?" — you're going to practice exactly that in the next modules.

1e62353a69eaf9: The debate over whether morality depends entirely on culture, or whether there are principles that apply to all human beings.
0c385f7f864c31:
The starting observation

It's an undeniable fact: different cultures and different points in history have had different moral codes, sometimes radically opposed ones. Moral relativism concludes from this that there is no objective or universal morality — what's right is simply whatever each culture considers right.

The argument in its favor

Relativism has a real virtue: it promotes humility toward other cultures, and avoids the historical mistake of imposing one civilization's values on another while assuming moral superiority without questioning it.

The most commonly raised problem

⚠️ The classic problem: if relativism were completely true, we couldn't say that historical practices like slavery or genocide were morally wrong — we could only say "they didn't match our current values." Most people, even those who value cultural tolerance, feel that there are lines that really were objectively crossed, no matter what that era's society thought.

A middle position: minimal universalism

Many philosophers today defend a middle position: there are some principles that seem to hold in practically every known human culture — like the idea that suffering inflicted for no reason is bad, or that gratuitous cruelty isn't celebrated in any stable society — while other norms (etiquette, customs, rituals) really are genuinely relative to culture.

🌍 A useful example of the difference: which food is "rude" to refuse at a dinner is relative to culture. That torturing a child for fun is wrong doesn't seem to be — practically no documented culture has openly defended it as a good thing.
💡 This distinction — between genuinely cultural norms and principles that seem more universal — is useful for thinking carefully instead of falling into "everything is relative" or "my culture is always right."

1fb178390c83c4:
The trolley problem

A runaway trolley is about to run over 5 people tied to the tracks. You're next to a lever: if you pull it, the trolley diverts to another track where only 1 person is tied down. Do you pull the lever?

🚋 Most people say yes — sacrificing 1 to save 5 seems right. This is consistent with the consequentialist/utilitarian reasoning from class 2.

The variant that changes everything

Now imagine you're on a bridge over the tracks, next to a very large stranger. If you push him, his body stops the trolley and saves the 5 people, but he dies. Same math — 1 life for 5 — but most people say they would not push him.

⚠️ Why does the answer change if the numbers are identical? Many philosophers point to Kant's deontological distinction: in the first case, the death is an unintended side effect of diverting an already-existing danger; in the second, you're actively using a person as an instrument — as a means, not an end — to achieve the outcome. Deontology explains that intuition better than pure consequence-calculation.

Why this isn't a pointless game

Trolley dilemmas aren't looking for a "winner" among the schools — they're meant to reveal that our moral intuitions are more complex than any single theory can fully capture. That's valuable information: it tells you serious moral reasoning needs more than one tool.

💡 A real exercise: next time you face a hard decision, ask yourself this course's three questions: what outcome does it produce? what rule am I following or breaking? what kind of person does this make me? If all three answers agree, your decision is more solid than if it depended on just one.

185c02b24ed58d:
Old dilemmas, new contexts

Modern technology creates situations the classic ethical schools never anticipated in detail — but their reasoning tools are still useful for thinking them through.

The self-driving car and the real trolley

A self-driving car must decide, in a split second, how to react to an unavoidable accident: does it protect its passengers or minimize total harm, even if that puts the people inside at risk? It's, literally, the trolley problem from class 6, programmed in advance in code instead of decided in the moment.

🤖 The uncomfortable question: should a company program its cars to minimize total deaths (consequentialism), or to never deliberately sacrifice its own passengers (a deontological rule)? Different manufacturers and countries have taken different stances.

Privacy, surveillance and consent

Kant's deontology — treating people as ends, not means — is central to the debate over personal data: using someone's information without their genuine consent to train systems or sell advertising is, in Kantian terms, treating that person as a means to someone else's benefit.

Algorithmic bias

When an AI system trained on historical data reproduces past discriminatory biases, consequentialism asks "what harm does this cause to the affected groups?", while virtue ethics asks "what kind of society are we building with this tool?" — both questions are necessary.

💡 No single school fully resolves these dilemmas on its own — but thinking with this course's three tools gives you a more precise vocabulary than "it feels wrong" or "it feels right" for taking part in these conversations, which are going to define a good part of your adult life.

0e5e4ac5ceb977:
What you covered

You started by distinguishing ethics from morals (class 1), saw the three major schools — consequences (class 2), duties (class 3), and character (class 4) — the relativism debate (class 5), how those schools clash in real dilemmas (class 6), and how to apply them to modern technology (class 7).

The goal was never to give you answers

If you finish this course expecting it to tell you "this is right, this is wrong" for every situation, the course failed its purpose. The real goal was to give you three different questions you can ask yourself facing any hard decision:

  1. What outcome does this produce? (consequentialism)
  2. What rule or duty am I following or breaking? (deontology)
  3. What kind of person does this make me? (virtue ethics)
🧭 Why use all three: when all three questions point in the same direction, you have a morally solid decision from several angles. When they conflict — like in the trolley problem — at least you know exactly WHERE the tension is, instead of just feeling discomfort you can't name.

One final honesty

2400 years of brilliant philosophers haven't resolved these debates definitively, and neither did this course. That's not a failure of the field — it's the real nature of the hardest moral questions. What you did gain is the ability to think about them more rigorously than before you started.
